verification.note: Citation (volume, issue, season and pages) checked in Sangster’s 2011 notes; the double issue is dated Fall 1996 there and April 1996 in Crossref. Text not read (the York journal site blocks automated access). Described only as a defence of gender history against Sangster’s dichotomy (Q36); the respondents’ theoretical positions are not characterised. Checked against: Sangster’s own bibliography and notes in Through Feminist Eyes (AU Press, 2011), read at https://read.aupress.ca/read/through-feminist-eyes/section/ae126747-ec01-4cc4-aeee-9e4bf07caa1e and the introduction (note 133); Crossref DOI record (no pages); answers/verification.json Q36. Addendum 2026-10-14: Addendum 2026-10-14 (Claude, Parr draft): read in full in an Internet Archive capture (15 February 2020) of the journal PDF (article/download/6970/6154). Pages 239–48 by running head. In n. 2 (p. 240) she quotes Parr's 'Gender History and Historical Practice' (in Parr and Rosenfeld, eds., Gender and History in Canada, 1996, p. 11) and says it tends 'to locate critics of gender history, feminist and anti-feminist alike, in the same oppositional group'. In n. 3 (p. 240) she notes she was reproached for not offering 'more criticism of historians such as Mariana Valverde and Joy Parr'. On p. 244 she quotes Parr (p. 14) that the move to gender 'began from the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships', adding that the two 'have blossomed in tandem'. She concedes she had 'congealed and possibly blurred two issues' (p. 244). She questions 'the prevailing assumption that gender history as the field, post-structuralism as the method, equals a superior, more broad-minded history' (p. 246; n. 14 cites Parr p. 21).

verification.note: Abstract read: thirty years of women’s labour history shaped by feminist, left and labour organizing, international social theory and Canadian historiography; feminist challenges to the initially ‘masculinist’ shape of working-class history, and calls to integrate race and ethnicity, shifted its narrative and paradigms; gender more effectively though not completely integrated into class formation; post-structuralism and the decline of the left unsettle the field. Checked against: Crossref DOI record; OpenAlex abstract (English and French). Addendum 2026-10-14: Read at pp. 130 and 133 and searched for Kealey in the journal's PDF (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/5205) for the 1.138 Kealey draft. p. 130 n. 8: Kealey (1995, p. 125) on two overlapping cohorts of the 1960s and 1970s; p. 133: 'One of the first major collections of the new labour history contained not one article on women' (Kealey and Warrian, Essays, 1976); 'Two seminal studies followed by Gregory Kealey and Bryan Palmer. Though differently positioned politically, they examined workers' responses to 19th century industrialization, with a proclivity to centre on skilled male workers and their actions in the public sphere'.

relations.relationship: Uses feminist critiques to reconsider gender, race and ethnicity within accounts of working-class formation.
relations.evidence_note: Reuse of the recorded abstract and bounded 2000 essay readings. The field’s masculinist starting points are Sangster’s diagnosis. This does not infer a single causal genealogy from political organizing.

relations.relationship: Questions treating women’s history and gender history as opposed stages in an inevitable methodological succession.
relations.evidence_note: The 2011 introduction’s own retrospect supports this formulation; existing addenda separately record full readings of the two original essays. The disagreement and Sangster’s concessions remain situated, not an assertion that all gender historians held one position.
